clinicalPearls: Congenital absence of the pericardium ranges from a small localised foramen to complete bilateral absence; partial left-sided defects are the most common form encountered clinically.

It results from premature atrophy of the left common cardinal vein (duct of Cuvier), which compromises the blood supply to the developing pleuropericardial membrane, hence the predominance of left-sided defects.
Most patients are asymptomatic and the diagnosis is made incidentally; when symptoms occur they are typically positional atypical chest pain, palpitations or dyspnoea.

Complete absence is usually benign, but partial defects carry the risk of herniation and strangulation of a cardiac chamber (especially the left atrial appendage) through the rim of the defect, which can be life-threatening.

Chest radiography classically shows leftward shift of the cardiac silhouette with a prominent pulmonary artery/left atrial appendage and interposition of lung between the aorta and pulmonary artery or beneath the heart.
The ECG often reveals rightward axis, poor R-wave progression and incomplete right bundle branch block due to cardiac displacement and rotation.

Echocardiography can be technically difficult and may show unusual windows, exaggerated cardiac motion and apparent right ventricular enlargement; CT or MRI is the definitive means of demonstrating the defect and any lung interposition.

Asymptomatic complete defects require no treatment, whereas symptomatic or partial defects at risk of herniation may warrant surgical pericardioplasty, defect enlargement or, occasionally, left atrial appendage excision.
reference.pathophysiology: During embryogenesis the pleuropericardial membranes, which are nourished by the left duct of Cuvier (common cardinal vein), grow to separate the pericardial from the pleural cavity. Premature involution of this venous channel deprives the left pleuropericardial membrane of its blood supply, so that it fails to develop fully; the consequence is a partial or complete, usually left-sided, pericardial defect. In complete absence the heart is abnormally mobile within the thorax and shifts leftward, but haemodynamics are generally preserved. In a partial defect the free edge of the residual pericardium can act as a constricting ring: a portion of the heart, most often the left atrial appendage, may herniate through and become incarcerated, leading to strangulation, myocardial ischaemia, arrhythmia or sudden death. The abnormal position and rotation of the heart account for the characteristic radiographic and electrocardiographic findings.
additionalDifferentials: atrial septal defect or other left-to-right shunt (from radiographic pulmonary artery prominence)
right ventricular volume overload of other cause
mediastinal or cardiac mass displacing the heart
acquired pericardial defect after surgery or trauma
arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (given apparent RV enlargement)
dextroposition of the heart from pulmonary or pleural pathology
additionalInvestigations: cardiac MRI (definitive demonstration of pericardial absence and lung interposition)
ECG-gated cardiac CT (defect delineation, chamber herniation)
chest radiography (leftward cardiac shift, lung interposition signs)
transthoracic echocardiography (abnormal windows, exaggerated cardiac swing)
12-lead ECG (rightward axis, poor R-wave progression, incomplete RBBB)
screening for associated anomalies (bronchogenic cysts, congenital heart disease, pulmonary sequestration)
exercise or ambulatory monitoring if positional symptoms or arrhythmia are reported
redFlags: positional or exertional chest pain with syncope suggesting chamber herniation or strangulation
new arrhythmia in a patient with a known partial defect
evidence of left atrial appendage incarceration on imaging
haemodynamic instability with abrupt severe chest pain
sudden cardiac death in a young person with an undiagnosed partial defect
reference.prognosis: Complete absence of the pericardium generally carries a benign prognosis and normal life expectancy, whereas partial defects have a less predictable course because of the risk of chamber herniation and strangulation, which can be fatal but is preventable with timely surgical correction.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the displaced cardiac silhouette and RV prominence as an atrial septal defect or right ventricular pathology.
Assuming all pericardial defects are benign and overlooking the herniation risk specific to partial defects.
Attributing technically difficult or unusual echocardiographic windows to poor acoustic access rather than the underlying defect.
Failing to search for associated congenital anomalies once the defect is identified.
Delaying surgical referral in a symptomatic partial defect until an acute strangulation event occurs.

management: Manage complete or asymptomatic defects conservatively with observation, as haemodynamics are generally preserved
Undertake surgical correction of partial defects, by pericardioplasty, primary closure or extension of the defect, to prevent herniation and strangulation of the left atrial appendage
Provide symptom-directed treatment for positional atypical chest pain and palpitations
Arrange cardiac imaging surveillance with MRI or CT to characterise the defect and monitor herniation risk
Escalate to urgent cardiac surgery if features suggest chamber incarceration or strangulation, such as acute chest pain, ischaemia or arrhythmia
Screen for and manage associated anomalies including bronchogenic cysts, congenital heart disease and pulmonary sequestration, with cardiology and cardiothoracic surgical input
